ch20.note: The essayist. This afterword (kaisetsu) is not by Shiba but by Muramatsu Takeshi (1929–1994), a critic and scholar of French literature who taught at several universities and, from the 1960s, was a prominent conservative commentator. A signed critical essay commissioned for the paperback reissue, the kaisetsu is a standard feature of the Japanese bunko edition. Muramatsu dates this one to March 1965.

ch20.anchor: the Chūgai Nippō, a Buddhist newspaper
ch20.note: Chūgai Nippō: a Kyoto daily, founded in 1897, devoted to Buddhist and religious affairs. Owl's Castle ran in it as a serial in 1958–59 before Kōdansha issued the novel in book form.

ch20.anchor: the Tachikawa Bunko invented the character of Sarutobi Sasuke
ch20.note: Tachikawa Bunko was a series of cheap pocket storybooks published in Osaka from about 1911 into the 1920s, retelling heroic adventure tales for boys. Sarutobi Sasuke, its most famous creation, is a fictional Kōga ninja in the service of the warlord Sanada Yukimura; more than any other single figure he fixed the popular image of the superhuman, shape-shifting ninja that the twentieth century inherited.

Murayama Tomoyoshi (1901–1977) was an avant-garde painter, stage director, and novelist of the political left. His Shinobi no mono (1960–62) recast the Iga ninja in Marxist terms as an exploited underclass; a bestseller, it became a long-running film series (released abroad as Band of Assassins).

ch20.anchor: Yamada Fūtarō wrote The Kōga Ninja Scrolls
ch20.note: Yamada Fūtarō (1922–2001) was a phenomenally prolific popular novelist. Kōga Ninpōchō (1958–59; translated as The Kōga Ninja Scrolls) launched his celebrated series of erotic-grotesque ninja fantasies, in which rival ninja clans meet in tournaments of outlandish secret arts.

ch20.anchor: known as a "master of ninja fiction."
ch20.note: The Japanese label plays on bungō, the word for a great man of letters, swapping in the character for "ninja" — so, half in jest, a "grand master of ninja fiction."

ch20.anchor: the eighth Kōdan Club Prize for a story called The Persian Sorcerer
ch20.note: The Persian Sorcerer (Perusha no genjutsushi) was Shiba's breakthrough story, winner of the eighth Kōdan Club Prize, an award of the publisher Kōdansha for popular fiction. Muramatsu dates it to 1955; the story in fact appeared in 1956.

ch20.anchor: among them The Xiongnu of the Gobi
ch20.note: The Xiongnu of the Gobi (Gobi no Kyōdo). The Xiongnu were the nomadic steppe confederation that dominated the Gobi in the age of Han China; "the Western Regions" (Saiiki) is the classical name for the lands of Central Asia along the Silk Road. Shiba had read Mongolian at the Osaka School of Foreign Languages, and several of his early stories draw on that world.

ch20.anchor: the Naoki Prize for the second half of 1959
ch20.note: The Naoki Prize is Japan's foremost award for popular fiction, given twice a year in tandem with the Akutagawa Prize for literary fiction. Owl's Castle won the forty-second, for the second half of 1959; it was announced early in 1960.
Kamigata Bushidō (1960), a later Shiba novel. Kamigata is the old name for the Kyoto–Osaka region, whose shrewd merchant temper supplies the book's theme.

ch20.anchor: Ishihara Shintarō's Season of the Sun
ch20.note: Ishihara Shintarō (1932–2022), novelist and, later, a combative governor of Tokyo. Season of the Sun (Taiyō no kisetsu, 1955) won the Akutagawa Prize and named the taiyōzoku, the "sun tribe" of affluent, rebellious postwar youth.

ch20.anchor: the protagonist of Yoshikawa Eiji's Miyamoto Musashi
ch20.note: Yoshikawa Eiji (1892–1962) was the most widely read historical novelist of his generation. His Miyamoto Musashi (serialized 1935–39; translated into English simply as Musashi) told the life of the swordsman — glossed earlier in this book — as a long parable of self-discipline, and shaped his modern image. The two women who attend Musashi in the novel are the gentle, faithful Otsū and the passionate Akemi, both named below.

Burn, O Sword (Moeyo ken, 1962–64) is Shiba's novel of Hijikata Toshizō and the Shinsengumi, the swordsmen's corps that policed Kyoto for the shogunate in its last violent years. Its founding rule, shidō daiichi, "the warrior's code before all," demanded absolute samurai bearing of a membership drawn largely from farmers.

ch20.anchor: In The Man of Demonic Cunning, too, the author writes the life of the rationalist genius Ōmura Masujirō
ch20.note: The Man of Demonic Cunning (Kibō no hito, 1963) is Shiba's life of Ōmura Masujirō (1824–1869), the physician turned military planner who built the new imperial army and was assassinated for it. Kawai Tsuginosuke (1827–1868) was the reformer and commander of the Nagaoka domain, who armed it with modern guns and led it to destruction resisting the imperial forces in the Boshin War; Shiba later made him the hero of a separate novel, Tōge (1966–68).

ch20.anchor: Saitō Dōsan, the predatory warlord of the Warring States who seized his master's house
ch20.note: Saitō Dōsan (c. 1494–1556), remembered as the "Viper of Mino": the very type of gekokujō, the low overturning the high. Tradition has him rise from itinerant oil-seller to lord of a province by supplanting his own master — hence Muramatsu's parallel with the modern corporate raider. He opens Shiba's Kunitori monogatari (1963–66).

ch20.anchor: worked at a newspaper, the Sankei Shimbun
ch20.note: The Sankei Shimbun is a national daily based in Osaka. Shiba (whose real name was Fukuda Teiichi) worked there for years as a reporter and cultural editor before he could live by his fiction.

ch20.anchor: His Bakumatsu, a set of biographies of assassins
ch20.note: Bakumatsu (1963), a set of linked stories about political assassinations in the turbulent last years of Tokugawa rule; bakumatsu is the standard name for that period, roughly the 1850s and 1860s.

ch20.anchor: the historical biographies of Kōda Rohan
ch20.note: Kōda Rohan (1867–1947), one of the giants of modern Japanese letters, who in his later years gave himself to painstaking shiden, works of documentary historical biography.

Sakaguchi Ango (1906–1955), an iconoclastic writer of the postwar burai-ha, the "decadent school." The Second-Rate Man (Niryū no hito, 1947) is his wry portrait of Kuroda Yoshitaka (Josui), the brilliant strategist whom history, and his own lord, left forever in the second rank.
